Listen to this article Share On Thursday, 27th January, 2011, J.K. Randle International hosted a SECURITY SUMMIT (Land; Air; and Sea) which focused on the security challenges which were already festering in Nigeria. The venue was the huge new banquet hall of Eko Hotel and Suites, Victoria Island, Lagos. The turnout was truly amazing as papers were delivered by security experts not only from Nigeria but from different parts of the world. The presence of Nigerians from the diaspora and their very robust scholarly contributions provided solid proof that their sojourn in foreign parts had not blunted their patriotic zeal. The National Security Adviser, General Owoye Andrew Azazi, CFR, was the Guest of Honour; and the Chief of Army Staff, Lt-General Onyeabo Azubuike Ihejirika who was represented by GOC 18 Division (Lagos) (General Officer Commanding) Brigadier-General K.T.J. Minimah, who later became Chief of Army Staff. Afterwards, all attempts to ensure that the recommendations were followed with ACTION fell on deaf ears. The only outcome was the award of a N10 billion contract to a Chinese company for the installation of CCTV Cameras in Abuja. Here we are, fifteen years afterwards, the contract appears to have gone the way of so many abandoned projects. The House of Representatives has resolved to investigate the $460 million closed-circuit television (CCTV) project awarded to a Chinese firm (ZTE Corporation) for surveillance in Abuja, following concerns that the system has remained non-functional despite Nigeria servicing the loan obtained for it. This followed a motion of urgent national importance that was moved on Wednesday by Amobi Ogah (LP, Abia) during the plenary, where lawmakers decried the continuous repayment of the loan obtained for the abandoned security infrastructure. It appears to have joined the list of Nigeria’s Abandoned Projects. A Colossal Waste of Resources. “Nigeria’s infrastructure deficit is made worse by countless abandoned or failed projects, leading to severe economic losses. Key national projects such as the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, East-West Road, and the Abuja Millennium Tower remain incomplete, wasting billions of naira. Successive administrations often neglect or abandon these projects, leading to inefficiency and wasted resources. With over 56,000 abandoned projects valued at an estimated N17 trillion, a systematic approach to project management is urgently needed. We must reflect on the scale of this waste, the reasons behind it, and potential solutions, including a national policy for the continuity of projects across administrations.” However, before the year ended, two incidents jolted our nation. The first was the attempt to assassinate the Inspector-General of Police Hafiz Ringim. Terrorists followed his convoy right into Louis Edet House, the Police Headquarters in Abuja. The first suicide bombing in Nigeria’s history occurred on 16 June 2011, when a suicide bomber drove a car bomb onto the premises of the Louis Edet House in Abuja, the headquarters of the Nigeria Police Force. He may have been trying to kill Inspector-General of Police Hafiz Ringim, whose convoy he followed into the compound, but he was stopped by security before he could do so. It was confirmed that the bomber and a traffic policeman were killed, although authorities said there may have been up to six casualties. It was the first suicide bombing in Nigeria’s history. A suicide bomber named Mohammed Manga drove a car bomb into the premises of the police headquarters. The second was the bombing of the United Nations office in Abuja. One of the casualties was Sarah Feese, the daughter of a former Minister of Works and Housing, Mr. Ambrose Feese. The United Nations House in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, home to 26 UN agencies and programmes, was struck by a car bomb on 26 August 2011. A total of 23 people were killed. Eleven were UN staff, including one international staff member. More than 80 were wounded. A bomb blast ripped through the United Nations offices in the Nigerian capital of Abuja, heavily damaging the building and killing at least 18 people, after a car rammed into the building, crashing through two security barriers. The United Nations Security Council issued a statement denouncing as a “heinous crime” the bombing of the UN headquarters in the Nigerian capital, Abuja, that killed at least 18 people. The August 26 car bombing was claimed by Boko Haram, which is described as a radical Muslim sect that has been waging a sectarian battle against Nigeria’s central government. Boko Haram is translated from the Hausa language to mean “Western education is sinful.” UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said 26 UN humanitarian and development agencies were housed in the compound. Hundreds of people were at work there at the time of the attack. Ban described the attack as an assault on those who devote their lives to helping others, and said the UN condemned it “utterly.” Ban added that the attack would not deter the UN from doing vital work for the people of Nigeria and the rest of the world.
